newsitem.title: THAILAND: Gasoline glut forces Thai Oil to diversify.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline glut forces Thai Oil to diversify.

text.p: Thai Oil Co Ltd, operator of Thailand's biggest refinery, said on Wednesday that it would diversify into more non-oil businesses as the local refined oil market was hit hard by surpluses and rampant oil smuggling.
Kasame Chatikavanij, Thai Oil chairman and managing director, said the company had no plans to expand its refinery capacity of 220,000 barrels per day (bpd).
With the coming onstream of two other new refineries last year, Thailand's local refining capacity now stands at around 760,000 bpd.
This does not include products from the Thai Petrochemical Industry Plc condensate splitter which operated at a capacity of 65,000 bpd.
Among non-oil projects that Thai Oil was already involved in or would be in the near future were carbon and petrochemicals production and power generation.
"Our petrochemical project like the mixed xylenes project will help reduce potential negative impacts from oil surpluses," Kasame told reporters.
The company's mixed xylene plant, at a refinery site in eastern Sri Racha, has started operation and products were expected to be lifted in February.
Mitsubishi in December signed an agreement to buy 150,000-200,000 tonnes of mixed xylenes annually from the firm.
Instead of selling gasoline at a comparatively low export price, Thai Oil would now be able to separate mixed xylene from platfomate and sell them as petrochemical feedstock, Kasame said.
The project would also help Thai Oil minimise its exports which it aimed to keep below five percent of all output for fiscal 1996/97 (October-September).
"We don't want to export at all because there are no incentives. It's the situation that forces us to," Kasame said.
Despite a tough market, the Thai Oil was able to record gross profits of 1.005 billion baht in 1995/96 -- a 200 percent rise from that posted in the previous fiscal year.
Kasame attributed the strong performance to higher prices, a temporary drop in regional refining capacity and the company's ability to effectively minimise foreign exchange risks.
On the crude procurement front, Thai Oil had no plans to substantially change its crude slate for 1996/97, according to Yiem Chundprasit, the firm's deputy managing director.
"We will import around 170-000-180,000 barrels per day of crude, 60 percent of which will be from the Middle East and the rest from the Far East," he said.
"We are not very interested in the crude from Africa due to freight disadvantage," he added.
